title: Edge trace adapter: OTLP intake translator with schema negotiation, batching & multi-backend failover
creator: Ayesha Kapoor
description:
Context:
Redwood's hosted tracing ingest must accept a wide variety of OpenTelemetry producers (older SDKs, custom exporters, proto vs. json over http) and reliably forward to downstream backends (Tempo primary, Jaeger for some customers). We need an edge adapter that sits in front of existing export pipelines to: negotiate/normalize schemas, perform cheap enrichment (tenant id mapping, sampling markers), correct common timestamp drift, and batch/forward to the appropriate backend with fast fallback for transient errors.

Goals:
- Provide a transparent OTLP intake translator that accepts gRPC/HTTP/OTLP-json and normalizes to a single internal envelope.
- Negotiate per-tenant schema versions and apply field mappings for legacy clients.
- Implement adaptive batching with size/time thresholds to hit 95th percentile end-to-end latency budget for small traces (<10 spans) while improving throughput for high-volume customers.
- Multi-backend routing: prefer Tempo, fall back to Jaeger or durable S3-like blob sink on sustained backend failures.
- Emit rich observability metrics (ingest latency, batch sizes, rejections, backend failover counts) and traces for our own pipeline.
- Minimal memory overhead and backpressure strategy to avoid head-of-line blocking in the proxy.

Non-goals:
- Full trace reassembly for very large batched clients (handled by downstream services).
- Replacing existing tenant auth; adapter reads existing tenant header and validates token via token-service but does not implement full auth.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Ingest adapter accepts OTLP/gRPC and OTLP/HTTP-json and normalizes to internal envelope for 99% of test producer variations.
2) Schema negotiation test harness can map two legacy clients' fields to the canonical schema with transformations (tag renames, timestamp correction).
3) End-to-end p50 latency for small traces remains <= 55ms and p95 <= 225ms under baseline load (10k traces/s).
4) When tempo-backend is artificially failed, adapter routes to declared fallback (jaeger endpoint) within 1s and increments failover metric.
5) Metrics emitted to our monitoring pipeline and a Grafana dashboard created with ingest rate, batch size distribution, backend error budget, and queue depth.
6) Security review sign-off and load test report attached to ticket.
design_notes:
- Use a lightweight stateful worker pool keyed by tenant to allow per-tenant schema caches while bounding memory.
- Schema negotiation: cache parsed mapping rules (JS-like templates) per tenant; fallback to best-effort field forwarding when unknown.
- Batching: hybrid policy (max_batch_bytes=512KB, max_batch_spans=500, max_delay_ms=40) tuned by experiments.
- Backpressure: use ring buffer per-tenant with drop-policy=oldest_small_traces to protect high-value single-span traces. Expose 'reject' metric for monitoring.
- Fallback logic: exponential backoff with jitter; after N failures escalate to durable sink and alert.
- Healthchecks: readiness only when schema cache warmed and backend connectivity healthy.
- Observability: instrument with otel-internal spans; tag spans with adapter_version, tenant_hash, route_target.
- Security: decrypt tenant keys via KMS integration; rotate keys using existing credential-rotation service.
open_questions:
- How many legacy schema mappings do we expect to onboard in Q2? (affects cache sizing)
- Should we support on-the-fly mapping rule updates via the Console or require config deploys?
- What's the acceptable drop-rate during sustained overload for low-priority tenants?
- Do we want to expose per-tenant ingestion SLA in Console tied to dedicated capacity?
implementation_plan:
Phase 1 (Spike, 1 week): small POC that accepts OTLP/HTTP-json, normalizes to internal envelope, and forwards to a local Tempo instance. Build basic metrics.
Phase 2 (Core work, 3 sprints): implement schema cache, per-tenant worker pool, batching policy, backend router and failover. Add tests and load harness.
Phase 3 (Hardening & rollout, 1 sprint): security review, key rotation integration, observability dashboard, gradual rollout behind feature flag for 5 pilot tenants.
Phase 4 (GA): enable by default and document configuration for private/dedicated deployments.
testing_plan:
- Unit tests for all mapping and normalization logic.
- Integration tests: OTLP/gRPC + OTLP/HTTP-json -> adapter -> Tempo/Jaeger test clusters.
- Load tests: 50k traces/s sustained with mixed sizes; run soak for 4 hours and capture latency/error metrics.
- Chaos test: induce tempo failures and validate failover metrics and routing.
- Security tests: KMS key rotation simulation and unauthorized header rejection.
- Regression tests for legacy mapping edge cases (missing timestamps, truncated attributes).
rollout_plan:
- Deploy behind feature-flag in staging and run verification harness.
- Canary: enable for 3 low-traffic tenants for 24 hours with alerting on error rate/latency.
- Expand to 20 tenants over 72 hours if stable.
- Monitor dashboards and rollback if backend error budget > 5% for more than 15 minutes.
- Post-mortem template ready in shared drive for incident notes.
